title: Pyrography Celtic knotwork panel
subtitle: Pyrography: a four-strand Celtic knotwork design burned on an oak panel
excerpt: A four-strand Celtic knotwork border burned onto a 20 cm square oak panel, with shading inside the strands to create a three-dimensional appearance. Celtic knotwork is an intermediate pyrography subject because the design requires accurate transfer, the over-and-under strand sequence must be maintained, and the shading inside the strands is blended rather than line-work.
sourceNotes: Traditional Celtic knotwork patterns from Cassell's Book of Drawing and Design (1899); four-strand border construction from the same source.

glossaryTerms.definition: The technique of burning designs into wood using a heated metal tip.
Building up areas of graduated tone by making overlapping passes with the pen tip at consistent speed, covering an area progressively rather than using single-line strokes.
Carbon-coated paper used to transfer a drawn design to a wood surface.

content.text: to burn an interlace design: four strands woven over and under each other in a continuous pattern. The difficult part is keeping track of which strand passes over which through the transfer and the burn. A clear method for this is given below.
Ventilation: pyrography produces wood smoke. Work near an open window or use a fume extractor. Do not burn in an enclosed room.
Hot tip: a pyrography pen tip is as hot as a soldering iron (200, 400 °C). Never touch the tip. Set the pen down on its stand when not actively burning.
Fire: keep the pyrography unit and workpiece clear of flammable materials. Do not leave the unit unattended when switched on.
First aid: a burn from a pyrography tip is a contact burn. Run under cool water for 20 minutes. Burns larger than a 5p coin go to A&E.

One seasoned oak panel, 20 cm × 20 cm, 10, 12 mm thick. Oak burns at a higher temperature than lime and the hard/soft ring contrast creates an interesting texture within the shaded areas of the strands. Sand to 240 grit.
Pyrography pen with a writing tip for the outline and a shading or ball tip for shading inside the strands.
Transfer paper and a printed or drawn Celtic knotwork reference.

Use a four-strand border knotwork pattern: four parallel strands that loop over and under each other in a regular sequence around the border of the panel. Before transferring, mark each crossing point on the reference image: draw a small 'over' indicator (a tick above the crossing) at each point where a strand crosses over its neighbour. This map of over-and-under is your reference during burning.

. Burn the outline of each strand in full, including where the strand passes under another strand. Then go back and break the under-strand line at each crossing to indicate that it passes below: erase these under-strand sections with a light pencil cross so you know not to burn them, or simply identify them from your over-under map and skip over them with the pen tip.

Inside each strand, shade the under-side edge: the edge of the strand that passes below the crossing strand is shaded darker. This gives the illusion of depth, the lighter upper surface and the shaded under-edge read as a round cord in three dimensions. Use a

tip at medium heat, moving the pen slowly in short overlapping arcs inside the strand edge. Build up the shading in layers, going over the area two or three times rather than trying to reach the final tone in one pass.
Wipe off carbon residue with a barely damp cloth. Apply one coat of clear wood wax or Danish oil. The shaded knotwork will deepen in tone and contrast considerably after finishing.

attrs.symptom: The knotwork over-and-under logic was lost during burning, the strands look like flat ribbons rather than interlaced cords
attrs.cause: The under-strand breaks at crossing points were not marked clearly enough before burning, or the shading on the under-side edges was skipped
attrs.fix: The under-strand gap cannot be added after burning, but the three-dimensional effect can still be produced by shading: go over the under-side edge of each strand with a light shading pass. Even without the outline gap, the graduated shading reads as depth.
